content.title: About
content.content: Puri is a traditional Indian bread made from whole wheat flour, water, salt, and sometimes a small amount of oil. The dough is rolled into small circles and deep‑fried in hot oil until golden. Puri has a light, airy interior and a crisp exterior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Puri is often served at breakfast with vegetable curries, chutney, or yogurt.
The dough is typically unleavened, making the preparation quick.
In some Indian regions, whole‑grain flour and spices such as cumin or coriander are added to the dough.
Puri can be made in bite‑size portions or larger ones, depending on regional customs.
Traditionally, puri is fried in a deep, heavy‑bottomed pan, but any deep‑frying skillet works today.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Puri provides steady energy through slowly digestible carbs, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains plant protein
items.content: Wheat flour supplies a modest amount of protein useful for tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour contains B1, B2, and B3 vitamins that support metabolic processes.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: When made with whole‑grain flour, puri adds dietary fiber that promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Frying in a small amount of vegetable oil adds a dose of monounsaturated fats.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Deep‑frying makes puri calorie‑dense; those watching weight should limit portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Puri is made from wheat flour and is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Risk of overeating
items.content: The crunchy texture and aroma can encourage rapid overconsumption.

items.title: Trans fats from reheating
items.content: Repeated reheating in oil may create trans fats, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve puri hot, straight from the oil. Dip them in chutney, yogurt, or sauces, or use them as a base for "puri‑burgers" with vegetables and meat. In some regions they are split and filled with spiced potatoes or legumes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked puri in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 1‑2 days. For longer storage, freeze them in bags and reheat quickly in an oven or skillet before serving.
